rates across the economy: loans, bonds, and savings accounts all carry rates — one line each
the honest framing: interest rates are a price, and like any price they change

the risk-free rate (short-term U.S. government borrowing) as the low-risk benchmark for the base rate
the prime rate as a base rate banks use to price loans

claims.claim: An interest rate is the price of borrowing money, expressed as a percentage rate over a period of time. Investor.gov's glossary defines interest as 'the price paid for borrowing money,' expressed as a percentage rate over a period of time; OpenStax frames the same idea as the 'rental price of money' set in a market for loanable funds; CFI describes an interest rate as the amount charged by a lender to a borrower for debt, generally expressed as a percentage of the principal.

Interest exists because lenders are compensated for time and for risk. CFI: interest is charged as compensation for lost opportunity — the lender could have invested the money elsewhere instead of lending it. OpenStax: the reward for delaying consumption is the real return to saving, and lenders want to be rewarded for credit risk, charging a premium to riskier borrowers.

A quoted rate can be read as a stack of pieces: a base rate, a risk premium, and an inflation expectation. OpenStax: the short-term U.S. government rate is often called the risk-free rate and serves as the low-risk benchmark; the prime rate is one of several base rates used to price loans; lenders charge a credit-risk premium to riskier borrowers (corporate and credit-card borrowers pay more than the government); and part of the nominal interest a lender receives compensates for inflation. CFI: interest rates are proportional to borrower risk, and lenders charge higher rates to compensate for the decline in purchasing power from inflation.

Rates move with market forces: in the market for loanable funds, savers supply money, borrowers demand it, and the equilibrium interest rate is where the two meet. OpenStax: the equilibrium rate is determined by the intersection of supply of and demand for loanable funds; a higher rate encourages lenders to supply more and is associated with lower quantities demanded by borrowers. CFI: an increase in demand for credit leads to a rise in rates; a rise in the supply of credit leads to a decline.

Rates move with central-bank policy: the Federal Reserve's primary means of adjusting monetary policy is changing its target for the federal funds rate — the rate banks pay to borrow reserve balances overnight — and changes to that target are rapidly reflected in the interest rates banks and other lenders charge on short-term loans to households, nonfinancial businesses, and government entities.

Higher rates make borrowing costlier and saving more rewarding. The Fed: when the FOMC reduces its target, the resulting lower rates on consumer loans elicit greater spending on durable goods such as automobiles, and lower mortgage rates make buying a house more affordable — the reverse holds when policy tightens. OpenStax: a higher interest rate encourages lenders (savers) to supply a larger quantity of loanable funds.

Interest rates appear across the economy: on loans, on bonds, and on savings. OpenStax examples: a 5.5% four-year auto loan, credit-card rates higher than corporate borrowing because credit-card loans are higher risk, a 6% savings-account rate, and the three-month U.S. government rate as the risk-free benchmark. CFI: the interest rate can also refer to the rate a bank pays its clients for keeping deposits.

Rates may be fixed or variable (floating). Investor.gov: interest rates may be fixed, meaning the rate is set and will not change, or variable or 'floating,' meaning the rate may move higher or lower over time. CFI: floating rates fluctuate based on a reference rate.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Framings of the definition differ across sources: Investor.gov calls interest 'the price paid for borrowing money'; OpenStax calls the interest rate 'the rental price of money' determined in a market for loanable funds; CFI calls it the amount charged by a lender to a borrower, expressed as a percentage of the principal.
positions: Interest as the price paid for borrowing (Investor.gov)
Interest rate as the rental price of money in the loanable funds market (OpenStax)
Interest rate as the amount charged by a lender to a borrower (CFI)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The framings are complementary views of the same price. The lesson uses Investor.gov's wording as the working definition (attributed) and folds in OpenStax's rental-price and CFI's lender-charge framings as supporting views.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Who sets rates: popular accounts often say 'the Fed sets interest rates,' while the Fed describes targeting a short-term policy rate that then ripples into other rates, and OpenStax/CFI describe supply and demand in the loanable funds market as the determination mechanism.
positions: The central bank sets interest rates (popular shorthand)
The Fed targets the federal funds rate; changes ripple into other short-term rates (Federal Reserve)
Rates are determined by supply of savings and demand for borrowing (OpenStax, CFI)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents both mechanisms factually: central-bank policy as a driver of short-term rates and market forces as the broader pricing mechanism. No forecasting is offered.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Inflation's role in rates: OpenStax and CFI both state that part of a nominal rate compensates the lender for inflation, but they present it with different arithmetic (real rate equals nominal minus inflation, with different worked numbers).
positions: Part of nominal interest compensates the lender for inflation; the rest is the real cost of borrowing (OpenStax)
Higher inflation leads to higher rates because lenders must be compensated for lost purchasing power (CFI)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names the inflation expectation as one component of a rate, in one line, and defers inflation mechanics and real-versus-nominal arithmetic to the inflation sibling topic. No formula is presented.
